Bachelor thesis · method briefing
Harm trees for health‑tracking apps
From attack trees to Knabenhans et al.’s harm analysis, a worked example on a constructed period tracker, and where a language model can help
core functionality
digital context
implementation choice
30 October 2026
The problem
To call a harm “missing”, you first need the harms that could happen
The question
What harms do providers of health-tracking apps communicate, and how do they present them?
The gap in it
A policy that never names a harm says nothing by itself. Silence only counts if the harm could arise from the app’s features.
The tool
Reference harm trees: pathways from data and features to capabilities to harms, written down before any policy is read.
Supervisor, 13 October: identify capabilities through the literature review, and synthesise a harm tree for the “best app” (what “best” means is still open, D12).
Thesis Sections 4.1 and “Reference Harm Trees”; supervisor meeting notes, 13 October 2026, §3 and “Harm tree”
Step 1 · The ancestor
Attack trees: a goal, broken into ways to reach it
Schneier (1999) puts the attacker’s goal at the root. Each child is one way to reach its parent.
OR: any one child is enough. AND: every child is needed.
Leaves can carry values, such as possible or impossible, or a cost, that are passed up to the root. A defence helps when it cuts every branch to the goal.
Goal: read a user’s cycle history
OR
Use the unlocked phone
Break into the backup account
Seize the phone
AND
Backup is switched on
Obtain the password
Schneier, “Attack Trees”, Dr. Dobb’s Journal 24(12), 1999 · not yet in the project corpus: check before citing · tree constructed for this deck
Step 2 · From attacks to harms
Privacy harm trees move the root from the attacker to the person
Attack tree
Root: what an attacker wants. Asks: how can the system be attacked? Source: Schneier 1999.
Privacy harm tree
Root: a harm to people. Asks: how can the system lead to that harm? Source: De and Le Métayer 2016 (smart grids), refined for reuse in 2017.
Knabenhans et al. build on these trees [16, 17]: they show the pathways to a harm and the root causes of each pathway, in any system (§1, §4.1).
De and Le Métayer, IEEE S&P Workshops 2016, 58–65; APF 2017, 52–83 · cited as [16, 17] in Knabenhans et al. 2026 · originals not yet in the corpus
Step 3 · What counts as a harm
A harm is measured against how life would otherwise go
CyberPeace Institute 2024, used by Knabenhans et al.
An “impairment or disruption of an entity’s capacity or ability to function”, compared with its usual context.
Individuals, groups or society; well-being, reputation, dignity, freedom or any other fundamental right.
Baseline in the paper
Current practice in the EU, where the digital identity framework is not yet widely used.
Baseline in the thesis
The user’s situation without the modelled pathway: the same person, without that flow of data.
Knabenhans et al. 2026, §4.1 (p. 6) and §4.2, citing CyberPeace Institute 2024 [14] and Citron and Solove 2022 [11] · thesis, “Harm Categories”

Citron and Solove: seven kinds of privacy harm
Kind
Pages
What it covers (subtypes named in the article)
Physical
831–834
Bodily injury or death made possible by personal data
Economic
834–837
Monetary losses and loss of value
Reputational
837–841
Injury to a person’s reputation and standing
Psychological
841–845
Emotional distress; disturbance
Autonomy
845–855
Coercion; manipulation; failure to inform; thwarted expectations; lack of control; chilling effects
Discrimination
855–859
Disadvantaging people on the basis of their characteristics
Relationship
859 ff.
Damage to relationships of trust, personal and professional
Knabenhans et al.’s list keeps six of them, adds societal harms, and leaves out relationship harms. The thesis adds them back as a tag.
Citron and Solove, “Privacy Harms”, Boston University Law Review 102 (2022) 793, Part V, pp. 830 ff. · Knabenhans et al. 2026, App. A · thesis, “Harm Categories”
Knabenhans et al. 2026 · the setting
Is privacy technology enough to make the EU digital identity safe?
The system
Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 sets up a digital identity wallet: issuers give credentials, users show attributes such as “over 18” to relying parties. The promised safeguard is privacy by design, with PETs such as anonymous credentials.
What the paper does
§3 formal model of the best privacy-by-design version §4 harm trees: age verification, driving licence §5 three capabilities every such system has
Finding: PETs reduce what flows, but many harms stay, because they come from the functionality or its digital context.
Knabenhans, Veitch, Raynal, Stadler, Chatel, Lueks, Troncoso, “On the (Privacy) Harms of the European Digital Identity Framework”, Cryptology ePrint 2026/867, abstract and §1
Knabenhans et al. §4.1 · the tree
Three levels: harm, capability, component
Harm at the top
OR
Capability that enables it
Capability, or an incapability
OR+
AND
Component · core
Component · context
Component · core
Component · implementation
OR any one child is enough · AND every child is needed · OR+ one or several children, possibly together
Knabenhans et al. 2026, §4.1 “Constructing trees” and Fig. 4 (p. 6) · generic tree drawn for this deck
Knabenhans et al. §4.1 · harm origins
Each leaf says where a pathway comes from, and who could cut it
Core functionality · black
What the minimal function leaks or requires, such as the relying party learning a function of the age. Not removable without the function.
Digital context · blue
What comes from using the function online: cookies, fingerprinting, advertising identifiers.
Implementation · red
A design decision, such as a persistent identifier in a naive implementation. Here PETs and design changes can act.
Mobile driving licence: no pathway depends on a red component, so privacy technology cannot cut any of them (§4.3).
Knabenhans et al. 2026, §4.1 “Harm origins”, §4.2 (age verification) and §4.3 (mobile driving licence)
Knabenhans et al. §4.2 · where the content comes from
Harms come from the literature; components come from the system
Harms
From studies of age verification (EDRi 2023; EFF 2023; Koning et al. 2014), extended with Citron and Solove and CyberPeace.
Seven harms, e.g. discrimination, structural exclusion, targeted advertising, censorship.
Capabilities and components
From the formal model of the functionality, the Commission’s use-case documents and the deployment requirements.
No completeness claimed: more harms only add evidence.
A health tracker has no specification: its components come from studies and from the app itself.
Knabenhans et al. 2026, §3, §4.1–4.2 (p. 7) and §4.4; references [11, 14, 24, 34, 46, 47]

Knabenhans et al. §5 · fundamental capabilities
Three capabilities come with the function itself
Distinguishing §5.1
Telling users apart by what they show, e.g. their nationality.
Tracker: separating users who log a pregnancy from those who do not.
Trackability §5.2
Linking the same user across different events.
Tracker: one device identifier sent with every analytics event.
Inference §5.3
Learning attributes that were never shown.
Tracker: a late period suggesting a pregnancy.
Defined as security games. The paper argues they follow from the functionality, so a PET can only limit them, e.g. by restricting what may be asked.
Knabenhans et al. 2026, §5.1–5.3 · tracker examples (blue) are this deck’s reading for health trackers, not the paper’s
Knabenhans et al. App. A · the harm categories
Seven categories, each with concrete examples
Economic
Loss through impersonation; locked out of one’s own bank account
Physical
Violence when a stalker learns an address; worse health from lost access to care
Psychological
Fear of being watched; distress after identity theft
Autonomy
Coercion, manipulation, limits on speech, information or movement
Discrimination
Profile-based discrimination; dynamic pricing
Reputational
Harm to reputation and dignity from records of what people do
Societal
Chilling effects and lost creativity under constant monitoring
Not in the list
Relationship harms: the thesis adds them as a tag

Transfer · the procedure
Building a reference tree, one step at a time
1 · Harms
List harms from the literature review (LQ1) and the App. A categories.
2 · Capabilities
For each harm, the capabilities that health-tracker studies document.
3 · Components
The data, feature and access each capability needs.
4 · Operators
Join them with AND, OR or OR+, and write down why.
5 · Origins
Tag each component core, context or implementation, argued from the studies.
6 · Per app
An applicability record: feature, evidence, assumption, decision.
Steps 1–5 follow Knabenhans et al. §4.1; step 6 is the thesis’s addition (Methodology, “Reference Harm Trees”; Appendix A, Steps 0–1)
Worked example · constructed app
CycleMate: a period tracker built for the example
What it does
  • Logs periods, symptoms, sexual activity, mood
  • Predicts the cycle and fertile window
  • Optional cloud backup
  • Shares identifiers and usage with analytics
  • Listing advertises “premium predictions”
U2
“We share device identifiers and usage data with analytics partners to improve our services. We never sell your health data.”
U3
“Your health data stays on your device unless you turn on backup. This keeps your reproductive health private and protects you from anyone using it against you.”
U9
“Because all predictions are calculated with encryption, no one can ever use your data to discriminate against you.”
Thesis Appendix A, “Worked Example” (codebook v4): app and policy are constructed and describe no real app · 3 of its 10 policy units shown
Worked example · Step 0
Five reference pathways for CycleMate
ID
Conditions (origin)
Capability
Harm
F1
Logged cycles (core) AND another person opens the unlocked phone (context)
Partner infers a possible pregnancy
Distress from unwanted disclosure; relationship tag
F2
Logged cycles (core) AND [cloud backup (implementation) OR seized phone (context)]
Authorities infer a pregnancy or a loss
Legal pressure, restricted reproductive choices (autonomy)
F3
Device identifier (context) AND analytics or advertising SDK (implementation)
Profiling across apps; sorted as “trying to conceive”
Different prices or offers (discrimination)
F4
Predictions offered only if the user agrees to sharing (implementation)
Core feature unusable without sharing
Restricted choice (autonomy)
F5
Cloud backup (implementation) AND an attacker gains access
Attacker reads the cycle history
Reputational damage or distress
A measure blocks a pathway only if it removes one of its necessary conditions. An app lock cuts F1; turning off backup cuts only one branch of F2.

Worked example · Step 4
Does the promised measure cut the pathway?
Unit
The claim covers
Reasoning against the tree
Decision
U2
Sale of health data
F3 runs through shared identifiers and usage data, not through a sale. The risk lies outside the claim.
no mismatch
U3
Protection from “anyone”, while backup is off
F1 is in scope: a person at the unlocked phone is “anyone”, and on-device storage does not remove that access.
potential mismatch for F1
U9
No one can use “your data” to discriminate
F3 leads to discrimination through the identifiers U2 says are shared. Encrypting predictions does not remove them.
potential mismatch for F3
U10
Nothing specific
No measure is named, so nothing can be compared.
not assessable
A potential mismatch is about the text: what it promises against what the named measure can do. It says nothing about the app’s real security.
Thesis Appendix A, Step 4, “The author’s review of CycleMate’s protection claims”
Worked example · Step 5
What one policy contributes to the research questions
RQ1 · coverage
2 of 4
applicable harms named as possible. Discrimination appears only as denied; reputational harm is not mentioned. Autonomy: uncertain, reported apart.
RQ2 · stance
5
stances on named harms: acknowledged; acknowledged and qualified; minimised; responsibility shifted; denied.
RQ3 · protection
2 of 3
claims flagged as potential mismatches (storage, encryption); the no-sale pledge is narrow. One unit is reassurance only.

Language models · the whole pipeline
Where a model helps, and where the author decides
B follows the thesis method (“LLM-Assisted Coding”, Appendix A Step 6); A and C are proposals for this deck and need a Decision Log entry before use
Proposal A · tree synthesis
From papers to pathways: the model drafts, the author verifies
Illustrative: capability categories K1, K2, K4 from the thesis’s capability table (literature-search v003 config); studies anonymised · precedent for span-grounded LLM annotation: Chanenson et al. 2025; Xie et al. 2025
B · coding policies (in the thesis method)
Every code must quote its evidence
{"unit": "U6",
"harm": {"code": "H-PSY",
"span": "you might experience unwanted contact"},
"stances": [
{"code": "S-ACK",
"reason": "the harm is presented as possible"},
{"code": "S-QUA",
"span": "In the unlikely event that …",
"target": "likelihood of the breach"}]}
Three stages
Find spans → stance per named harm → protection claim
A screener, not a judge
No span, no code. The author checks every harm mention; runs are repeated to measure stability.
Validated blind
Ten apps coded by hand first. A hit needs label, unit and span to match.
Thesis Appendix A, Step 6, and Methodology “LLM-Assisted Coding”, “Validation and Missed Mentions” · precedents: Wilson et al. 2016; Harkous et al. 2018; Rodriguez et al. 2024
Proposal C · checking a claim against the tree
Does encryption cut the discrimination pathway?
Reasoning from thesis Appendix A, Step 4 (U9, F3) · the model’s role here is a proposal; in the thesis method the author alone decides mismatches
From codes to conclusions
How a harm ends up in the results
1 · Applies
At least one pathway to the harm is applicable. Only uncertain ones: uncertain.
2 · Named
A checked code for the harm in the captured texts, with its status and stance.
3 · Sorted
Named as possible · only denied · no mention identified · uncertain, apart.
4 · Counted
Across apps, per category and surface: descriptive shares, no tests.
CycleMate, constructed
Named as possible: psychological; relationship tag
Only denied: discrimination
No mention identified: reputational
Uncertain, apart: autonomy
Conclusion for this policy: it names distress, denies discrimination, is silent on reputational harm, and two of its protection claims reach further than their measures.
Thesis Appendix A, Steps 1 and 5; Methodology “Analysis and Reporting” · “no mention identified” refers to the captured material only
Guardrails and open points
What stays with the author, and what is still open
Rules for the model
  • Never decides applicability or mismatches
  • No quoted span, no code
  • Every harm mention checked by hand
  • Model, prompt and run logged
  • Trusted only after the blind ten-app test
Still open
  • What the “best app” is (D12)
  • Read De and Le Métayer, Schneier
  • Check the Knabenhans version
  • Justify pathway fields, applicability
  • Record proposals A and C first
